chunks: "Motors and solenoids are inductive loads. Both are coils of wire, so electrically each is a resistance, the copper, in series with an inductance, the magnetic field of the coil.

What makes an inductive load different from a resistor is that its current can't change instantly: the voltage is L di/dt, so the current ramps up with time constant L over R, and when you turn it off it tries to keep the current flowing, which creates a big voltage spike across the switch, the flyback or inductive kick.
So you need a freewheeling diode or snubber. In AC the current lags the voltage, so there's reactive power and a power factor below one. A motor adds one more thing: back-EMF.
A spinning motor generates a voltage proportional to speed, so it behaves like R plus L plus a source that depends on speed.
That makes it a dynamic load: the current depends on the mechanical load and speed, high at stall and low at speed, and it can even regenerate.
A solenoid's inductance also changes as the plunger moves.
So the one-line answer is 'inductive, with a back-EMF for motors', and the design consequences are inrush at startup, flyback protection, and PWM current ripple set by the inductance."
